creator: Alan Flusser
note: The foundation: the rules and proportions of classic menswear. The creator calls it his starting point.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
chapters: Accessories: the major importance of minor things
contents.coverage: Adapting classic clothing to individual physique and complexion; coordinating patterns, choosing silhouettes and collars, and dressing for business casual and formal occasions.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Practical notes across 12 headings; formalwear thin. Core ideas corroborated by established reviews, finer rules mostly from reader notes.
knowledge.limits: No full chapters read. F3 is a secondary reader-note source, not a publisher excerpt. Its measurements and rules are reported advice, not independently authenticated text or universal fitting laws.

sections.summary: Start with the wearer, not seasonal fashion. The stable relationships of face, neck, shoulders, torso and legs are a better foundation than designer novelty. Interwar examples teach principles rather than require historical imitation. GQ notes that the book does not fully address modern casual lifestyles.

Keep attention on the face. F3 describes relating clothing contrast to actual hair/skin contrast and repeating natural pigments near the face. Strong contrast can support a high-contrast face but overwhelm a muted one. Assess the individual, not an ethnic category. Reviews corroborate complexion as a central concern, not every precise color prescription.

GQ quotes the relation between broader shoulders and fuller lapels. Collar-to-face, shoulders-to-head and jacket-to-leg relationships must be judged together. F3 says narrow shoulders exaggerate head size and broad shoulders diminish it. Cover the seat without needlessly shortening the apparent leg. There is no single fashionable jacket length appropriate to everyone.

F3 reports strongly different scales for two similar patterns; compatible scale for unlike patterns; and avoiding two tiny busy designs. With three similar patterns, graduate size from the shirt outward. With two similar and one unlike, separate the similar scales and relate the odd design to the prominent one. The aim is a readable whole, not showing how many patterns you can combine.

F1 reports 0.5-0.75 inch of shirt collar above the jacket collar. F3 says trouser volume should continue the jacket silhouette: fuller jackets with fuller trousers, closer jackets with slimmer legs. It favors trousers at the waist, charcoal as a versatile first business suit and navy as flattering. These are classic business priorities, not every wardrobe's needs.

Darker trousers can dress up a sport jacket. Color can unify separates: keep two of three pieces in the same family and relate the shirt through tone or contrast. A waistcoat adds gravity to single-breasted tailoring. This is an incomplete secondary account, not the full chapter.

Choose collar shape for the face. F3 describes spread points as a counterweight to a long narrow face, collar size relative to head size and collar height relative to neck length. Allow room to sit and raise arms without gaping or untucking. Cuffs should stay at the wrist, not slide over the hand. Smooth cloth and firmer collars read dressier; choose a blue that supports rather than overwhelms the face.

Tie width relates to lapels. F3 places the knot within the collar opening and the tip near the belt's upper edge. F1 specifically records the advised dimple. F3 limits bow width to the face/collar scale. Balance matters more than buying the fashionable width or largest knot.

Relate socks to trousers rather than make sock and shoe into an isolated block. Another option repeats a color or pattern from near the face. Finer hosiery suits more formal clothes; bulkier textures support heavier socks. The notes' restriction on black socks is a traditional preference, not a universal current rule.

F1 confirms smart shoes with tailored trousers. F3 describes a cap-toe Oxford for smart town wear, a blucher as less dressy and brown suede across seasons. Shape, formality, condition and relation to the trouser matter. Unsupported spending or leather-age claims are not adopted.

sections.section: Accessories: the major importance of minor things
sections.summary: Echo rather than exactly match a tie with the square. A lustrous tie can benefit from matte linen/cotton; a square can pick up a shirt or jacket color. Keep the effect unstudied. Belt color follows shoes and then the outfit, with a simple buckle. Details support the whole rather than pull attention away from the face.

The review confirms distinctions between dinner-jacket and full-dress details. Reliable actual chapter rules were not recovered. Rules from another book or a generic black-tie guide are not substituted and labeled Flusser.

A shared color family holds unmatched separates together; a patterned shirt can repeat a jacket/trouser color. F4 questions the longevity of a near-monochrome polo-and-corduroy example. The 2002 chapter's coordination logic travels better than every outfit or workplace assumption.

note: Commentary on wardrobe pieces, their history and how to wear them. The creator returns to Boyer’s ideas often.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.
contents.coverage: Alphabetically arranged essays on wardrobe pieces, traditions, fabrics, patterns, colors and how to use them, combining history with practical style advice.

knowledge.scope: Original summaries, not full text or a substitute for the book. Missing chapters and evidence limits are explicit.
knowledge.depth: Substantive or historical notes on 24 of 26 essays, with uneven depth. Boots and dressing gowns unverified; shorts and craftsmanship remain thin.
knowledge.limits: Established reviews corroborate the core philosophy; much chapter detail relies on two openly posted reader-note sources, not an official complete preview. Care advice remains subject to garment labels and professional judgment.

sections.summary: The name comes from the Ascot race meeting and its pinned silk neck scarf. B4 presents soft silk/light cashmere at an open collar as an alternative to a bare neck. This establishes a tradition and option, not the entire essay.
No reliable substantive account of this essay was recovered.
Boyer prefers a self-tied rather than pre-tied bow. Its irregular natural shape belongs to wearing it, rather than requiring factory-perfect symmetry.

Clothes communicate membership and context. Aim to let others judge your work instead of your outfit. Simplicity and comfort matter; head-to-toe designer outfits and conspicuous matching can erase individuality. B3's country-jacket/jeans and Barbour/suit examples illustrate mixing genres, not what every office permits.

Quality may cost more initially but last longer. The essay's craft discussion includes Thomas Girtin's Makers of Distinction and Richard Sennett's The Craftsman as reading. No full construction checklist was recovered.
The essay moves from workwear to youth rebellion, including Brando in The Wild One. Clothing carries a social language beyond its material. No complete fit/wash advice recovered.
No reliable substantive account of this essay was recovered.

Accumulated, lived-in clothes and patina suggest continuity rather than a freshly purchased coordinated costume. Sturdy country fabrics and pieces of different ages can look at ease together. The point is an unforced whole, not mandatory shabbiness.

Matching coat/trousers, uncuffed hems and an outside stripe related to lapel facings make a coherent tuxedo. The silk bow relates to those facings. Plain dark hosiery and simple black footwear keep focus on the wearer. The notes list calf/patent Oxfords and formal slippers as options; this is not the complete essay.

Frames should fit within the face width, sit below eyebrows and above cheeks, and stay securely on the bridge. They support the intended impression without becoming the main subject. Optical fit and prescription requirements still need an optician.

Know scent type and strength; use a restrained amount in business and lighter scents in heat. Test on skin and wait before judging. Avoid sun, unsealed storage and extreme temperatures. Aim for a clean presence rather than a scent cloud.
Facial hair is personal choice within professional context, not a blanket requirement to shave. Relate beard/moustache volume to face size so it does not become a detached dominating feature.

Lighter construction can retain shape. The account connects Armani's reduced padding with comfort and describes the lighter Neapolitan approach. It distinguishes more sober northern business dress from playful combinations. National generalizations do not prescribe every person's style.

Oxford button-down, khakis, Shetland sweater and loafers form an adaptable core. Tweed/navy blazer, flannel suits and seasonal suits increase formality. Edge stitching is one jacket marker. The lesson is a compatible vocabulary, not an obligatory shopping list.

Rotate and air clothes; brush tailored cloth, fold knitwear, use proper hangers and shoe trees. Avoid needless dry cleaning/pressing; use cautious heat and a protective cloth if the garment permits. Sleeve/trouser adjustments are unlike rebuilding shoulders/collar/chest: buy near a good base fit. Follow the actual care label before applying any technique.

Personality and deliberate choice matter more than rigid correctness. Clothes complement you; quality matters; refusing a distracting purchase is part of style. Avoid displaying money, accessories or rule memorization.

Prevent one garment dominating. Vary scales so pieces remain legible. Subtle pattern against pattern can integrate an outfit better than isolating one loud design against stark solids. Judge the whole, not a pattern count.
Restrained silk gives business dress a small accent; white linen/cotton is a simple formal option. Tie and square echo rather than exactly match. A related color is more relaxed than a matching set.

B1 reports smaller collars for smaller men and higher collars for longer necks. B4 relates knot size to tie space, collar stiffness to formality and sleeves so about half an inch of cuff shows. Treat collar/tie/square as one chest composition; exact matching can look labored.

Boyer objects to sockless business suits with dress shoes. B4 describes footwear as either continuing the leg line or deliberately breaking it, with darker shoes coherent against trousers and brown offering tonal variety. This is not a ban on all sockless casual wear.
The essay connects shorts to military/sporting dress. Its actual length, styling and occasion advice was not recovered.

Conceal effort, rather than be ignorant or careless. A little rumple or unforced genre mixing can look more convincing than flawless coordination. Do not mechanically add a contrived mistake; ease comes from understanding what you wear.

A commissioned waistcoat adds variations, pockets and temperature flexibility. Peak lapels are the traditional double-breasted choice. The notes establish selected ideas and historical development, not a complete fit/fabric manual.

Linen, breathable wool and deliberately rumpled seersucker have different useful behaviors. Choose for climate and cloth performance rather than demand permanent sharp pressing. The essay treats wrinkles as compatible with summer ease.
A turtleneck with a suit is permitted as deliberate nonchalance in a suitable setting. Its bohemian associations are discussed. It does not replace required formal attire at every occasion.

Bonded rubber/cotton, tightly woven treated gabardine and waxed cotton are distinct traditions. Waxed cloth requires renewed wax. Heritage and material history do not establish a modern technical waterproof rating.

contents.scope: Contents and coverage only; no full book text.

contents.coverage: Ten chapters, a black-tie brand directory and a Stephen Fry foreword. Covers classic and contemporary evening wear, outfit/accessory examples across levels of formality, and the future of the dress code.
contents.caveat: The official preview page was found, but its contents pages were not readable in this check. Do not treat this coverage summary as a complete table of contents.

knowledge.depth: Detailed practical topic notes from official companion guides. Direct book evidence limited to its philosophy and ten-chapter structure.

sections.summary: Black tie evolves. The book respects traditional tenets while emphasizing the effort made for special occasions. It presents different formality levels and alternatives. This is not permission to ignore an invitation's actual expectations.

Single-breasted one-button peak/shawl and double-breasted alternatives are presented. Silk lapel facings and jetted pockets distinguish eveningwear from business suits. M3 rejects notch lapels as a house preference. M2 calls no vents traditional but permits other vents, and relates broader lapels to double-breasted balance.

Satin is smooth and reflective; grosgrain ribbed and more matte. M2 relates finer ribs to curved shawls and stronger ribs to peaks; self-facings suit velvet/less overtly formal jackets. M3 discusses barathea and wool-mohair. Its body praises midnight blue but FAQ favors black. That conflict is not turned into a single rule.

Higher rise and enough leg volume support a clean vertical line. Classic trousers match jacket cloth with silk outside-seam trim and uncuffed hem. M3 excludes belts, favors braces and recommends waistcoat or cummerbund, not both. Its blanket waist-covering statement does not explain double-breasted exceptions; these are not inferred as book content.

Marcella/piqué fronts provide formal texture with studs; pleated fronts add texture with studs or suitable buttons; covered plackets offer quiet minimalism. The aim is differentiation from a daily business shirt. Full collar/cuff advice not recovered.

A self-tied silk bow relates to lapel facing; a simple white square and socks covering skin when seated complete the outfit. M2 favors coherent studs/cufflinks over competing details. Its shirt-studs subsection is visibly incomplete, so not summarized.

Tartan with velvet, checks with off-white jackets and velvet-on-velvet are presented as alternatives. White trousers are called summer-only and nontraditional. Smoking/velvet jackets suit some less strict events. Distinguish experimentation from the classic uniform and follow the invitation.

Ready-to-wear fixes standard proportions; made-to-measure adjusts an existing pattern; bespoke creates an individual pattern through fittings. The site's preference for its own made-to-measure service is commercial, not an objective universal ranking. Ask what can actually be changed.

sections.summary: Early bespoke drew from the restrained English country gentleman's wardrobe. The publisher follows aristocratic to military patronage. This explains the prestige of sobriety and individual fit; complete monarch-specific chapter detail was not recovered.

House histories emerge through customers, including film clients of Anderson & Sheppard and naval associations at Gieves & Hawkes. Cut/reputation and social context are connected. Hawkes introduced immediate wear in 1929; its off-the-peg sales surpassed bespoke by 1948. The review names Richard Anderson, Ozwald Boateng and Richard James as a new establishment, and Edward Sexton, Spencer Hart and Timothy Everest in a renaissance. The institution changes commercially and stylistically rather than standing outside fashion.

sections.summary: Three years visiting workshops, factories and shops led to more than fifty selected houses. Jacomet rejects an exhaustive catalog or definitive academic history. It is a personal craft journey, including modest workplaces behind glamorous objects.

The Prandoni-derived ideal is sober and clear-lined, with structured shoulders, a fitted waist and high armholes. Teachers and apprentices transmit it. This distinguishes a geometric outline from softer approaches without supplying universal fitting measurements.

Caraceni's Roman approach uses lighter cloth and less shoulder padding than its British antecedents but retains structure: a geometric shoulder and broad-to-fitted-waist V. It is fluid without simply following natural shoulder contours. The story of Henry Poole garments reaching the family is explicitly a family legend.

The Attolini/Rubinacci account removes weight/internal support. Markers include natural shoulders, little or no lining, shirt-like sleeve insertion with small gathers, a curved boat chest pocket, patch pockets and overlapping cuff buttons. Sleeve fullness aids movement. Softness still requires skilled cutting; these are school markers, not obligatory features of every Neapolitan suit.

Vitale Barberis Canonico and cloth-mill histories appear alongside makers. Finished garments come from a cloth-making system, not just a label. Full mill profiles, fiber grades and fabric specifications were not recovered.

The interview uses Ciro Paone/Kiton to illustrate persistence when workshops were closing. The publisher identifies Rubinacci, Kiton and Zegna with continuity and quality. This is maker history, not an independent ranking or current construction guarantee.
Salvatore Piccolo's shirts/workshop illustrate the section. No full advice on collar proportion, stitches, shrinkage or fitting was exposed.

Marinella's friendliness, early hospitality and roots in Naples, including a declined overseas-shop offer, show service and identity within craft. Tie folds/construction, umbrellas and glove techniques remain unverified.

Enzo Bonafè's recollections of apprenticeship with Amedeo Testoni and shoes for Ronald Reagan show knowledge passed between people/generations. No complete lasts, welt or fit comparison was recovered.

creator: Klaus Klemp

title: Brett Whiteley: Art & Life
creator: Barry Pearce, with Bryan Robertson and Wendy Whiteley

The publisher emphasizes landscape, the nude and fluid drawing. This is the art survey, not Ashleigh Wilson's biography Art, Life and the Other Thing.

sections.section: 1. An Old and a New Tradition
sections.summary: Heisenberg opens with atomic weapons, then asks whether their political power is the deepest consequence of modern physics. His answer is that the new account of reality may outlast its immediate technology. As scientific methods move across cultures, they meet older religious and philosophical traditions rather than replacing them in one uniform way. Quantum theory is his main example because it breaks with classical assumptions about what exists, not merely because its mathematics is difficult. The chapter sets the book's project: explain that break in ordinary language and examine how a scientific way of thinking can enter different cultures.

sections.summary: The story begins with black-body radiation: Planck's energy quanta solve an experimental problem that classical physics could not. Einstein's light quanta, atomic spectra, Bohr's atom and the Compton effect make the conflict between particle and wave descriptions unavoidable. De Broglie extends wave-particle duality to matter; matrix mechanics and wave mechanics provide new mathematical descriptions. The uncertainty relations and Bohr's complementarity supply an interpretation of what those descriptions let us say. Heisenberg presents the 1927 Solvay debates as a hard test, not an effortless consensus. His larger point is that successful equations arrived through a decades-long struggle to change the concepts used to describe nature.

sections.section: 3. The Copenhagen Interpretation of Quantum Theory
sections.summary: Experiments must still be described with classical words such as position, momentum and apparatus, although their application to atoms is limited. Heisenberg separates preparing an experimental situation, evolving its probability function and making a new measurement. The function combines tendencies for events with information about the preparation; it is not a picture of a particle's definite trajectory between observations. His microscope and interference examples show why incompatible experimental arrangements cannot simply be combined into one classical image. Measurement joins a system to an apparatus and the wider world. He explicitly distinguishes this physical transition from the observer's mental act of registering it. The claim is not that wishing or consciousness manufactures reality.

sections.section: 4. Quantum Theory and the Roots of Atomic Science
sections.summary: Heisenberg compares modern atomic physics with Greek attempts to find unity beneath change. Democritus's atoms and void made matter intelligible through enduring building blocks. Heraclitus emphasized change; Plato and the Pythagorean tradition connected the structure of things to mathematical forms. Quantum particles do not behave like miniature permanent pieces of ordinary material, so the ancient materialist picture cannot be carried over intact. Heisenberg finds a closer analogy in mathematical form and in Aristotle's potentiality: possibilities have a role distinct from completed events. These are comparisons, not claims that the Greeks discovered quantum theory. Modern equations gain their authority from precise experimental tests that ancient speculation could not supply.

sections.section: 5. Philosophical Ideas Since Descartes and the New Quantum Situation
sections.summary: The Cartesian split between thinking subject and extended object helps explain the classical ambition to describe a world entirely apart from the observer. Heisenberg argues that quantum experiments make that clean division difficult to maintain. He considers empiricism, skepticism, positivism and Kant's claim that certain organizing concepts are necessary before experience is possible. Concepts inherited from ordinary life remain indispensable, but their usefulness does not establish unlimited validity. Space, time, causality and substance cannot be assumed to apply unchanged in every new experimental domain. He also resists a simple rule that every sentence not reducible to a narrow empirical test is meaningless. Scientific language is historically developed, powerful and revisable.

sections.section: 6. Quantum Theory and Other Parts of Natural Science
sections.summary: A physical theory can form a closed, internally connected system of concepts, as Newtonian mechanics does. A later theory does not make every earlier calculation worthless: classical mechanics remains effective within its domain. Heisenberg compares mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, relativity and quantum theory to explain why their concepts cannot always be exchanged without limits. Quantum theory supplies the basis for understanding chemical bonds where a purely Newtonian account failed. In biology he treats the relation between physical description and the language of living systems as a serious question, not a settled license for vitalism. He ends by comparing scientific conceptual systems with artistic styles: each makes aspects of reality expressible through a coherent human language.

sections.summary: Relativity provides an earlier warning that everyday concepts are not immune to experiment. The development from electromagnetic problems to Einstein's theory changes the treatment of simultaneity, space and time. Special relativity connects these in a single framework and connects mass with energy; general relativity gives gravitation a new geometrical description. Heisenberg cautions against declaring older philosophies simply disproved by particle annihilation: their word 'substance' is not identical to the physicist's measured mass. The important lesson is methodological. Even a precise, familiar concept can reach the edge of its applicability, and careful measurements can force revision. Relativity therefore prepared scientists to take the stranger conceptual changes of quantum theory seriously.

sections.section: 8. Criticism and Counterproposals to the Copenhagen Interpretation
sections.summary: Heisenberg examines attempts to restore a more classical objective picture, including hidden-variable proposals and objections associated with Einstein. He distinguishes alternatives that alter predictions from reinterpretations designed to reproduce the same observations. His defense emphasizes the consistency of quantum predictions and the symmetry properties he believes counterproposals compromise. He also discusses why treating system and measuring apparatus as one isolated quantum system does not by itself produce a definite recorded result. This is a partisan chapter: it states Heisenberg's case for his interpretation, not a neutral survey of a settled modern debate. The strength of experimental quantum mechanics should not be confused with proof that every philosophical conclusion he draws is compulsory.

sections.section: 9. Quantum Theory and the Structure of Matter
sections.summary: The chapter follows successive reductions of apparent complexity: chemical elements are organized through atoms, atoms through nuclei and electrons, and nuclei through protons and neutrons. Quantum theory explains why atoms have stable properties and why chemistry has its particular regularities. High-energy experiments then complicate the idea of a final set of indestructible building blocks, because particles can be created, destroyed and transformed. Heisenberg hopes for a unified mathematical scheme whose solutions give the different forms of matter. He discusses short-distance and time-order questions as problems for future research. This is a mid-century account with speculative endpoints, not a present-day guide to particle physics or a claim that his proposed unification succeeded.

sections.section: 10. Language and Reality in Modern Physics
sections.summary: Natural language is flexible enough to support discovery, but familiar images can mislead when applied outside the circumstances that formed them. Mathematical language offers precision; it does not remove the need to explain experiments in shareable ordinary terms. Heisenberg uses the changes in geometry and relativity, then wave-particle descriptions and quantum logic, to show the tension between rigorous formalism and intuitive pictures. Complementary descriptions may be useful even when they cannot be assembled into one classical story. His distinction between potentialities and facts is meant to prevent treating a quantum state as a hidden movie of already actual events. Clear speech requires stating what an experiment establishes and what an explanatory image merely suggests.

sections.section: 11. Modern Physics and the Development of Human Thinking
sections.summary: Heisenberg returns to the meeting of scientific and cultural traditions. He sees fruitful ideas emerging where lines of thought from different places and periods can genuinely interact. Modern technology carries scientific habits into societies that did not originate them, but it can also create disruption and weapons rather than automatic moral progress. He criticizes rigid materialist doctrines and argues for openness about the limits of scientific concepts, while recognizing that religious or cultural beliefs can function as a basis for life rather than as laboratory hypotheses. The desired outcome is tolerance and a connection between technical development and human values, not scientific conquest of every domain. These judgments belong to the book's historical and political setting.

title: Post Economic Society (essay by @erik_alan_norman)
creator: @erik_alan_norman
note: A three-slide text carousel (a LaTeX-style typeset PDF page, 3 pages) posted by @erik_alan_norman on 2026-10-11, titled "Post Economic Society" with author line "[insert ego here]", dated October 2026. Read directly from the three slide images. It is the creator's own speculative essay, not a published work; its claims are the creator's opinion and were not fact-checked. Argument in six sections: (1) the myth of meritocracy: pay tracks ownership and position in the capital loop rather than value creation, citing Piketty's r > g; (2) a 'poly-crisis' of three pressure points: a tech capex bubble (AI/quantum infrastructure spending without matching revenue), sovereign debt servicing under high rates, and a cyber attack on clearing systems as detonator; (3) the 'mycelial model': when the canopy collapses the fungal network redistributes nutrients, and the decentralized internet is the human equivalent; economic allocation becomes an engineering problem, with a comparison table (financialized capital vs 'post-hoarder mycelial model': distribute productivity gains to the workforce, optional volunteer-focused work, no false-merit rewards); (4) neurodivergent people (autistic, ADHD, trauma-adapted) as natural navigators of a post-collapse 'de-masking' shock; (5) labor realigned around intrinsic motivation: automation engineering of drudgery (closed-loop organic bioreactors, self-sustaining public utilities) plus low-frequency civic volunteer rotations for irreducible manual tasks; (6) pre-configuring the network now through neighbor-run elder-care (meals, medical transit, companionship). The caption asks 'What would that even look like? Why?' with tags #economics #economy #sociology #psychology #math. Four references are cited in the essay (items 224-227); a [3] Fisher entry is listed but only [1], [2] and [4] are cited in the text I read. Location tag: UCLA Math Sciences Building.

title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century
creator: Thomas Piketty (trans. Arthur Goldhammer)
note: Cited as reference [1] in the essay ("Harvard University Press, 2014"), used for r > g. Matches the publisher record: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, published 2014-04-15, translated by Arthur Goldhammer. Part and chapter titles below were checked against the contents page in the publisher's sample PDF; the summaries are original and not checked against the full text.

knowledge.scope: Original part-level study notes, not a substitute for the book.
knowledge.depth: Substantive summaries of all four parts (16 chapters grouped)
knowledge.limits: Part/chapter titles verified from publisher sample PDF contents page; summaries are original, from general knowledge, not checked against the full text. Not a full book text.

sections.summary: Sets out the basic concepts: national income, capital as the stock of wealth, the capital/income ratio and the capital share of income. Chapter 1 surveys output and income across countries, and chapter 2 argues that high growth (above 1-2% a year) is historically exceptional and driven by catch-up and population, so slow growth is the normal state and the future will look more like the past than the postwar boom.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: Part Two - The Dynamics of the Capital/Income Ratio (ch. 3-6)
sections.summary: Traces wealth over three centuries in Britain, France, Germany and the US. Capital stocks were about 6-7 years of national income before 1914, collapsed with the world wars, depression and taxation, and have been rebuilding. Piketty states his 'laws': capital share = r x (capital/income), and in the long run capital/income = savings rate / growth rate, so low growth pushes the ratio up. Chapter 6 discusses whether the capital-labor split is stable, with the elasticity of substitution as the key technical question.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: Part Three - The Structure of Inequality (ch. 7-12)
sections.summary: Chapters 7-8 compare how concentrated income and wealth are, using the 'two worlds' of Europe and the US. Chapter 9 explains the rise of very high labor income ('supermanagers') through pay-setting power, not marginal productivity. Chapter 10 shows wealth is far more concentrated than income. Chapter 11 argues inheritance's weight is returning towards nineteenth-century levels, with a 'rentier vs. supermanager' trade-off. Chapter 12 looks at global wealth inequality and the higher returns large fortunes earn. This is where the central inequality r > g does its work: when the return to capital exceeds growth, inherited wealth compounds faster than the economy and wages.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: Part Four - Regulating Capital in the Twenty-First Century (ch. 13-16)
sections.summary: Policy proposals: a modern 'social state' built on education, health and pensions; a more progressive income tax (with very high top rates); and the signature idea, a progressive annual global tax on capital with international transparency on bank data, as a realistic utopia. Chapter 16 treats public debt, favoring a capital tax or inflation over austerity to deal with it.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

title: Bullshit Jobs: A Theory
creator: David Graeber
note: Cited as reference [2] ("Simon & Schuster, 2018"), used for the essay's hobby-vs-job and drudgery sections. Matches publisher and reference pages: Simon & Schuster, published May 2018, expanded from Graeber's 2013 essay 'On the Phenomenon of Bullshit Jobs'. sections.summary: Defines the term: a job so pointless or pernicious that even the worker cannot justify its existence, yet who feels obliged to pretend otherwise. The test is the worker's own judgment, and Graeber distinguishes it from merely 'shit jobs' (badly paid, but useful).
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: 2. What sorts of bullshit jobs are there?
sections.summary: The five-part taxonomy: flunkies (make superiors feel important), goons (act aggressively for an employer, e.g. lobbyists, corporate lawyers), duct tapers (patch problems that should be fixed properly), box tickers (create the appearance that something is being done) and taskmasters (assign work to others who do not need supervision, or invent bullshit tasks).
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: 3-4. Why do people in bullshit jobs report being unhappy? What is it like?
sections.summary: Argues that the damage is psychological: loss of a sense of being a cause with an effect on the world, a kind of 'spiritual violence', and the burden of having to fake purpose. Draws on hundreds of testimonials.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: 5-6. Why are bullshit jobs proliferating? Why does society not object?
sections.summary: Locates the cause in 'managerial feudalism': the finance-driven economy and the political logic of creating loyal retainers and status hierarchies. Society tolerates it because of a work ethic that treats suffering at work as moral worth, so people resent others who have meaningful work.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.section: 7. What are the political effects, and what can be done?
sections.summary: Links bullshit jobs to resentment politics and argues for a universal basic income as one way out, to break the link between employment and the right to live.
sections.evidence: Original summary from general knowledge of the book plus the publisher/reference page; not checked against the book text.

sections.summary: Fisher's 'reflexive impotence': people know the system is broken but believe nothing can be done, so their knowing becomes part of the stasis. 'Business ontology' is the assumption that everything, including schools and hospitals, should be run as a business.

sections.summary: Argues the privatisation of stress: rising depression and anxiety are treated as individual chemical problems rather than social ones. Neoliberal 'market Stalinism' multiplies audits and targets, so bureaucracy is not removed but displaced into performance metrics. The state is used to defend corporate interests while public services are hollowed out.

sections.summary: The 2008 financial crisis cracked the facade. Fisher calls for making mental health a political issue, reviving the idea of a public sphere, and using small cracks to expose capitalism's inconsistencies and bring back a politics of the possible.
